title: Demonstrate an understanding of the nutrient requirements and fertilisation of vines

lessons.title: What nutrients vines need
lessons.html:
What nutrients vines need

Like people, vines need food to grow. Their food comes from the soil as nutrients, taken up by the roots with water. If a nutrient is missing, the vine grows badly and gives a poor crop. If there is too much, it can also cause problems.

Main nutrients

NutrientWhat it doesSigns of shortage
Nitrogen (N)Growth of shoots and leavesPale, yellow-green leaves; weak, short shoots
Phosphorus (P)Roots, energy, floweringPoor growth; sometimes dark or reddish leaves
Potassium (K)Ripening, sugar, water useLeaf edges turn yellow or brown and curl
Calcium (Ca) and magnesium (Mg)Strong cells; green colourMagnesium: yellow between the veins of older leaves
Boron, zinc, iron (trace elements)Needed in small amountsPoor berry set, small or yellow young leaves

Too much is also bad

  • Too much nitrogen makes a thick, leafy canopy, more disease and poor ripening.
  • Too much potassium can upset the balance of the wine.
  • Too much fertiliser washes into rivers and groundwater and pollutes them.

Soil acidity (pH)

Many Western Cape soils are acid. In very acid soil, roots grow badly and some nutrients are locked up. Lime is used to make the soil less acid. Soil tests show how much lime is needed.

How the farm knows what is needed

  • Soil analysis: soil samples are tested in a laboratory.
  • Leaf or leaf-stalk (petiole) analysis: leaves are picked at a set stage, often at flowering, and tested.
  • Looking at the vines: growth, leaf colour and crop size.

The manager or an adviser uses these results to make a fertiliser programme for each block.

lessons.title: Applying fertiliser correctly and safely
lessons.html:
Applying fertiliser correctly and safely

Types of fertiliser

  • Chemical (mineral) fertilisers: granules or soluble powders such as LAN for nitrogen, or mixtures with N, P and K. The numbers on the bag show the nutrient content.
  • Organic fertilisers: compost and manure. They feed the soil slowly and improve its structure.
  • Foliar sprays: nutrients sprayed onto leaves, often for trace elements.
  • Fertigation: fertiliser dissolved in the drip irrigation water.

When to fertilise

Vines take up most nutrients during active growth. The programme usually gives fertiliser in spring, some after flowering, and some after harvest so the vine can store food for next year. Follow the programme for each block exactly.

Spreading granular fertiliser by hand

  1. Check the block, product and amount on the instruction sheet.
  2. Use the measuring cup or scoop you are given, so each vine or metre of row gets the right amount.
  3. Spread evenly in the band where the roots are, under the drip line or along the vine row, as instructed.
  4. Do not throw fertiliser against the trunk or onto leaves; it can burn them.
  5. Do not spread before heavy rain is expected, or on water-logged soil.
  6. Irrigate after spreading if instructed, so fertiliser moves to the roots.

Record keeping

Write down the block, product, amount, date and who applied it. Records help the manager check the programme and are needed for export and quality schemes.

Safety and the environment

  • Wear gloves, overalls and a dust mask. Wash hands before eating.
  • Lift bags with bent knees; get help with heavy bags.
  • Store fertiliser dry, off the floor and away from fuel. Some fertilisers can burn or explode with heat or fuel.
  • Keep fertiliser away from rivers, dams and boreholes. Clean up spills.
  • Never mix fertiliser and chemicals unless the programme says so.

Key points

  • Vines need N, P, K, calcium, magnesium and trace elements.
  • Shortage and excess both cause problems; too much nitrogen gives a thick, leafy canopy.
  • Soil and leaf analysis guide the fertiliser programme.
  • Measure exactly, spread evenly in the root zone and keep fertiliser off trunks and leaves.
  • Wear PPE, store fertiliser safely and keep it out of water.
